stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a new fertilizer increases tomato yield. They have 40 garden plots available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of commute time (minutes) are:

**City A:** 10, 10, 12, 13, 16, 17, 21, 21, 22, 22, 23, 27, 27, 28, 29

**City B:** 17, 19, 19, 25, 25, 27, 28, 30, 31, 33, 33, 37, 38, 40, 73
In a randomized experiment on a new study strategy, 91 of 160 students using the new strategy passed a test, compared with 39 of 150 students using the usual strategy.

Data were collected on outdoor temperature (°F) (x) and daily iced-drink sales (y) for a sample of days. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    29.9
x           2.5
S = 4.4    R-Sq = 55.0%
```

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 57, s₁ = 13 and n₂ = 20, s₂ = 3. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Each sample contributes s²/n.
Variances add, even for a difference.

questions.stem: Each of 5 independent devices fails with probability 0.2. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: That is the probability all fail.
Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
That is the probability none fail.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 110 adults in a city, 42 use public transit weekly. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all adults in a city who use public transit weekly?

options.why: Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.96.
Divide by n inside the square root.
Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Multiply the standard error by z*.

questions.stem: A sample of 12 values is used for a one-sample t interval. Which condition must be checked because the sample is small?

options.why: That is for proportions.

options.text: The sample data show no strong skewness or outliers (population approximately normal)
options.why: Correct. Small samples need approximate normality.
That is for chi-square tests.

options.text: The sample size is at least 30
options.why: That is the large-sample alternative.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 89 and standard deviation 4. What value is at the 95th percentile?

options.why: Use the z-score for the percentile, not the percentile itself.
Check the sign of z.
Multiply z by σ, not σ².
Correct. z = invNorm(0.95) ≈ 1.645; x = μ + zσ.

questions.stem: For a distribution of household incomes in a city, the mean is 32 and the median is 40. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.

questions.explanation: Mean 32 < median 40: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A and B) = 0.09. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.18.
Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.18.
P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: For a distribution of number of social media followers, the mean is 80 and the median is 66. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: Correct. A long right tail pulls the mean above the median.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.

questions.explanation: Mean 80 > median 66: the mean is pulled toward the right tail.

questions.stem: Which variable is quantitative?

options.text: Whether a student owns a car (yes or no)
options.why: That is categorical.

options.text: The number of text messages a student sends per day
options.why: Correct. Counts are quantitative.
That is categorical.
Zip codes are labels.

options.why: Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.

questions.stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p > 0.4 gives a p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.why: Unrelated to the p-value.

options.text: There is a 0.03 probability that H₀ is true
options.why: A p-value is not the probability of a hypothesis.

options.text: If p = 0.4, there is a 0.03 probability of a sample proportion at least as large as the one observed, by chance alone
options.why: Correct. That is the definition of the p-value.

options.text: There is a 0.97 probability that Hₐ is true
options.why: Not a valid interpretation.

questions.explanation: That is the definition of the p-value.

questions.stem: If the sample size quadruples, what happens to the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄?

options.text: It is cut to one quarter
options.why: It depends on √n.
Correct. σ/√n: √4 = 2.
Larger samples reduce variability.
It depends on n.

questions.stem: Each of 10 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.5. What is the probability of at most 8 successes?

options.why: That is P(X < k); 'at most k' includes k.
That is only P(X = k).
That is the complement.
Correct. Use the binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.5.

questions.stem: Which statistic is an unbiased estimator of the population proportion?

options.text: The sample proportion p̂ from a random sample
options.why: Correct. Its sampling distribution is centered at p.

options.text: The largest proportion among several samples
options.why: That would tend to overestimate.

options.text: The proportion from a voluntary response sample
options.why: Voluntary response is biased.

options.text: The median of the sample values
options.why: Not an estimator of a proportion.

questions.explanation: Its sampling distribution is centered at p.

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 40 − 0.7x. An observation has x = 2 and y = 43.8. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.text: 5.2; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.
That is the predicted value ŷ.

options.text: -5.2; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.

options.text: 5.2; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 420 students at a large high school, 97 have a part-time job. Which is a 99% confidence interval for the proportion of all students at a large high school who have a part-time job?

options.why: Divide by n inside the square root.
Use z* for 99%, not 1.96.
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 2.576.
Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).

questions.stem: The slope of a regression line predicting exam score from hours studied is 3.5. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: A student who studies 0 hours scores 3.5
options.why: That would be the intercept.

options.text: 35% of the variation in scores is explained
options.why: That is r².

options.text: For each additional hour studied, the predicted exam score increases by about 3.5 points
options.why: Correct. Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

options.text: Each student's score increases by exactly 3.5 points per hour
options.why: The slope describes predicted, not actual, values.

questions.explanation: Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

questions.stem: The correlation between car age and resale price is r = -0.7. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: About 49% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

options.text: About 49% of the variation in resale price is accounted for by the linear model relating resale price to car age
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

options.text: Car age causes 49% of resale price
options.why: Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 70% of the variation in resale price is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: That is P(junior) overall.
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.
That is P(drives | junior).

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.02 at 95% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Square z*/m.
Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Always round up to guarantee the margin.
Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 1.96, rounded up.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.04 at 95% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Always round up to guarantee the margin.
Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Square z*/m.
Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 1.96, rounded up.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, and yes to generalizing to all students at the school

options.text: No to cause and effect, and no generalization beyond the volunteers

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, but only for the volunteers in the study
options.why: Correct. Random assignment decides causation; no random selection decides generalization.

questions.explanation: Random assignment: yes. Random selection: no.

questions.stem: To test H₀: p = 0.4 versus Hₐ: p > 0.4, a random sample of 370 gives p̂ = 0.48. What are the test statistic and p-value?

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the new fertilizer lead to a better total weight of tomatoes harvested than the standard fertilizer for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the new fertilizer vs the standard fertilizer). Response: total weight of tomatoes harvested.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 40 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–40; use a random number generator to select 20 different numbers.
Those 20 receive the new fertilizer; the remaining 20 receive the standard fertilizer.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by sun exposure (full sun or partial shade). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by sun exposure.

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.
Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether City B has any outliers. Show your work.

rubric.example: IQR = 12; upper fence = 37 + 1.5(12) = 55. Outlier(s): 73.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for City B (30) is greater than for City A (21).
City B is less variable (IQR 12 vs 14).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: City B has a high outlier, suggesting right skew.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for City B, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 31.7 is pulled toward the high value; median 30 is not.

parts.prompt: State hypotheses to test whether the new strategy leads to a higher pass rate.

rubric.example: H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0; Hₐ: p₁ − p₂ > 0, where p₁ and p₂ are the true pass rates with the new and usual strategies.

parts.prompt: Name the procedure and check the conditions.

rubric.criterion: Two-sample z test; random assignment; large counts with the pooled proportion.

parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
State a conclusion in context at α = 0.05, including what kind of conclusion the design allows.

rubric.criterion: Correct decision; causal language justified by random assignment.
rubric.example: Reject H₀: convincing evidence that the new strategy causes a higher pass rate (random assignment).

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 29.9 + 2.5x, where ŷ is predicted daily iced-drink sales and x is outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of outdoor temperature (°F), the predicted daily iced-drink sales increases by about 2.5.
About 55.0% of the variation in daily iced-drink sales is accounted for by the linear model with outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 4 and y = 44.6. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 39.9; residual = 44.6 − 39.9 = 4.7: the actual value is above the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of days from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
